headline: OpenAI drops GPT-6 Astra and claims the "AGI era" has arrived — meanwhile MSFT slipped 2% last night and PLS had another rough day on the ASX.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: MSFT had a rough night last session, sliding 2% to $499.70 USD. No single catastrophic news item drove it — the broader NASDAQ was soft, and some profit-taking after a strong AI-driven run seems to be the culprit. Microsoft's long-term cloud and AI story remains intact; this looks like normal fluctuation after a big run-up.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: Pilbara fell 2.1% today to close at $5.09, part of a broader sell-off across ASX lithium stocks. The sector is under pressure as lithium prices remain subdued and investor sentiment stays cautious. No company-specific bad news — it's the wider lithium market headwind dragging the whole sector lower.

movers.name: Global X AI ETF
movers.note: GXAI bounced 1.6% today to $16.44 — a welcome green day. The flood of new AI model releases from OpenAI, Google, Anthropic and Meta this week has reinvigorated enthusiasm for the AI sector, lifting the ETF. Still down 13% from your entry price overall, but today's move is a positive sign.

movers.name: Alphabet Inc. (Google)
movers.note: GOOGL dipped 1.1% last session to $335.31 USD. The market was slightly soft across the board on the NASDAQ, and some investors may be rotating attention toward Microsoft's Azure AI narrative. Alphabet's cloud growth and dividend continue to support the stock's fundamental value — a minor move in the context of its long-term trajectory.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Take-Two was essentially flat last session, up a modest 0.26% to $214.69 USD. GTA 6 is still the big catalyst everyone's watching — news this week about Rockstar editing the China trailer for local censorship rules is a reminder of the global commercial ambitions around the game's release. Still underwater on this position, but no new bad news.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market ETF
movers.note: VTS nudged up 0.42% to close at $529.04 today on the ASX — a quiet positive session tracking the broad US market. Nothing to worry about here; this is the kind of steady grind that makes it a solid long-term holding.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG edged up 0.21% to $77.03 today. Quiet and steady — exactly what you want from a diversified growth ETF. No news driving it specifically; just the broader market ticking along.

movers.name: Vanguard Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE gained a tiny 0.14% to $93.92 today. Emerging markets continue to grind slowly — no big moves either way. Long-term exposure to developing economies remains the thesis here, and nothing has changed that story.

watch_today.title: MSFT: Big dip last night — but sit tight
watch_today.detail: Microsoft fell 2% to $499.70 USD last session, wiping some recent gains. There's no structural problem here — the Azure cloud and Copilot AI businesses are growing strongly, and the stock has been on a big run. For a long-term holder, this is noise. Your position is still up 12.8% overall. Hold firmly.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX: Lithium sector still under pressure
watch_today.detail: Pilbara dropped another 2.1% today to $5.09, and your position is now down 24.5% overall. The lithium price cycle is the real story — it's still in a down-phase, and the whole ASX lithium sector is being dragged with it. If you believe lithium demand will recover (EVs, batteries), the long-term case is still there. But if you're feeling exposed, it's worth reviewing your conviction. For now: hold unless your thesis has changed.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX: Green day off the back of GPT-6 Astra launch
watch_today.detail: Your Global X AI ETF bounced 1.6% today, helped by massive AI news — OpenAI launched GPT-6 Astra, Google, Meta and Anthropic also shipped new models this week. Still down 13% from your entry, but the sector tailwind is real and strengthening. For a long-term AI believer, this could be a moment to consider topping up at a lower price.

watch_today.title: RBA rate hike on the table in September
watch_today.detail: UBS and Capital Economics are both tipping the Reserve Bank of Australia could raise interest rates at its upcoming September meeting. A former RBA official is also forecasting a 10% drop in house prices. A rate hike would put pressure on growth stocks and property — worth watching heading into the meeting. No action needed yet, but keep an eye on the RBA decision date.

watch_today.title: US midterms heating up — mail voting battle at the Supreme Court
watch_today.detail: The Trump administration is fighting to restrict mail-in voting ahead of the US midterms, with courts and now the Supreme Court involved. Political uncertainty in the US can create market jitters — worth monitoring as the situation escalates.

watch_today.title: GOOG: Dip last night, but fundamentals intact
watch_today.detail: Alphabet slipped 1.1% last session to $335.31 USD. Despite the noise around Microsoft and OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra, Alphabet's cloud growth and dividend provide a solid floor. Your position is up 9.1% overall. No reason to act — sit tight.

world.summary: The US-Iran conflict dominates global headlines, with Trump dismissing it as 'small potatoes' while intelligence reports warn Iran is deliberately dragging the conflict out to destabilise the US ahead of midterm elections. Separately, a major legal battle over mail-in voting is escalating toward the US Supreme Court.

stories.title: Trump calls US-Iran conflict 'small potatoes' as fighting continues
stories.why_it_matters: The US is engaged in an ongoing military conflict with Iran, but President Trump is publicly downplaying its severity, calling it 'small potatoes.' Vice President JD Vance has gone further, saying he 'wouldn't call it a war.' Meanwhile, US intelligence reports suggest Iran is deliberately prolonging the conflict to unsettle Trump ahead of November's midterm elections. Experts are divided on how the conflict could end, with no clear exit ramp in sight. For everyday people, this conflict is keeping oil markets elevated and adding to global economic uncertainty.

stories.title: Courts block Trump's mail-in voting restrictions as midterms approach
stories.why_it_matters: A federal judge has twice now blocked the Trump administration's efforts to restrict mail-in voting ahead of the US midterms. North Carolina has already started sending out mail-in ballots — the first state to do so. The Trump administration has escalated the fight to the Supreme Court, asking the justices to overrule the lower court. This is a major constitutional and electoral battle playing out in real time, with potential to shape control of the US Congress — which in turn affects US economic policy and markets.

stories.title: Iran planning to unsettle Trump ahead of midterms, intelligence warns
stories.why_it_matters: US intelligence agencies believe Iran is deliberately prolonging its conflict with America as a geopolitical strategy — specifically aiming to drain US resources and public patience before November's midterm elections, potentially costing Trump's party seats in Congress. This kind of calculated adversarial strategy adds a layer of political complexity to what might otherwise be seen as a straightforward military conflict. It also means the conflict is unlikely to end quickly, keeping energy markets and global risk sentiment elevated.

stories.title: Vance 'extremely skeptical' US strike hit Iranian wedding party
stories.why_it_matters: Reports emerged that a US military strike may have hit a wedding party in Iran, killing civilians. Vice President Vance pushed back hard, saying he is 'extremely skeptical' of those reports and refused to characterise the broader conflict as a war. This civilian casualty allegation is likely to intensify international pressure on the US and could complicate diplomatic efforts to de-escalate. It's the kind of story that tends to shift public opinion and add pressure on the administration.

stories.title: Middle East conflict drives 35% surge in overseas help requests from Hong Kong residents
stories.why_it_matters: The ongoing Middle East conflict has caused a 35% spike in Hong Kong residents seeking consular or emergency assistance from overseas, according to the South China Morning Post. It's a human indicator of how far the ripple effects of the US-Iran conflict are spreading — disrupting travel, business, and the lives of expats and diaspora communities far from the actual fighting. It underscores the broader global reach of what the Trump White House is calling 'small potatoes.'

markets.summary: The ASX 200 slipped a quiet 0.16% today to close just above 9,000. Last night on Wall Street, the S&P 500 and NASDAQ both edged lower — down 0.38% and 0.29% respectively — with tech stocks like MSFT and GOOG taking the biggest hits. Gold fell sharply by 1.4% last night, while oil was roughly flat. The Aussie dollar is holding steady around 72 US cents.

indicators.note: Quiet session, edging just lower. Broadly flat.

indicators.name: S&P 500

indicators.name: NASDAQ Composite
indicators.note: Last night — tech slightly soft; MSFT and GOOG dragged lower.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Essentially flat — Iran conflict keeping a floor under prices.

indicators.name: Gold

indicators.note: Steady around 72 cents — no big moves.

politics.summary: The RBA is under the spotlight with two major banks tipping a rate hike in September, while a former RBA official has predicted a 10% drop in Australian house prices. Separately, veterans' groups are criticising the Albanese government over how it treats ex-service members.

stories.title: UBS and Capital Economics tip RBA rate hike in September
stories.why_it_matters: Two major economic forecasters — UBS and Capital Economics — are now tipping the Reserve Bank of Australia will raise interest rates at its September meeting. If correct, this would push borrowing costs higher for anyone with a mortgage or business loan. Higher rates also tend to put downward pressure on the share market, particularly growth-oriented stocks. Keep an eye on the RBA's next meeting date — this is the most significant near-term economic risk for Australian households.

stories.title: Former RBA official forecasts 10% drop in Australian house prices
stories.why_it_matters: A former senior RBA official has publicly predicted that Australian house prices could fall by 10% — a significant warning from someone who knows the bank's thinking from the inside. The forecast is tied to the expectation of further rate rises making mortgages more expensive and cooling demand. For property owners and investors, a 10% correction would be substantial. For renters or first home buyers, it could eventually mean more accessible prices — but only after a painful adjustment period for the broader economy.

stories.title: RBA's inflation view out of step with Australians' lived experience
stories.why_it_matters: Economists and commentators are pushing back on the RBA's official inflation narrative, arguing the bank's models don't capture how hard everyday Australians are actually being squeezed. The RBA uses traditional economic measures like CPI, but critics argue real costs — groceries, rent, insurance, childcare — are rising far faster than the data suggests. This debate matters because if the RBA is miscalibrated, it risks either raising rates too aggressively (hurting households further) or not enough (letting inflation run hotter for longer).

stories.title: Veterans advocacy group accuses Albanese government of 'appalling' treatment of ex-service members
stories.why_it_matters: A veterans' advocacy column is accusing the Albanese Labor government of seriously mishandling the welfare of Australian veterans — covering issues like delays in claims processing, inadequate mental health support, and bureaucratic failures. Veterans' welfare has been a long-running political sore point across multiple governments. With an election cycle approaching, this kind of sustained criticism from military communities can become politically costly for Labor in marginal electorates.

ai.summary: This week has been one of the biggest ever for AI model releases. OpenAI launched GPT-6 Astra and is claiming we've entered the 'AGI era' — meaning AI that can match or exceed human performance across most tasks. Google, Anthropic and Meta all shipped major new models in the same week. The AI regulation debate is also hotting up globally.

stories.title: OpenAI launches GPT-6 Astra, claims 'AGI era' has arrived
stories.why_it_matters: OpenAI has released GPT-6 Astra and made the bold claim that the 'AGI era' — artificial general intelligence, where AI can do most things a human can do — has officially begun. The model reportedly brings major improvements in reasoning (thinking through complex problems step by step), coding ability, and computer use (it can control a computer to complete tasks on your behalf). This is a significant milestone claim, even if it's partly marketing — it signals the pace of AI improvement is not slowing down. For investors in AI-related stocks like GXAI and GOOG, it's a reminder that the sector narrative remains very strong.

stories.title: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta all ship new models in the same week
stories.why_it_matters: In an extraordinary week for AI, all four of the biggest players — OpenAI (GPT-6 Astra), Google (new Gemini), Anthropic (Claude Fable 5.1) and Meta — released major new models within days of each other. The 'same catch' referenced in coverage is that all of them come with significant safety caveats and ongoing scrutiny about what these systems can actually do reliably. The competitive race is clearly accelerating, which is good news for the AI ETF space but also raises questions about which company ultimately wins out.

stories.title: Jensen Huang, Sam Altman and Elon Musk push back on heavy AI regulation at G20 summit
stories.why_it_matters: The world's most powerful AI executives — Nvidia's Jensen Huang, OpenAI's Sam Altman, and Elon Musk — all appeared at the G20 technology summit and collectively warned governments against heavy-handed AI regulation. Their argument: too many rules will stifle innovation and let authoritarian countries (particularly China) get ahead. Critics counter that without guardrails, AI risks getting out of control. This debate will shape the regulatory environment that all AI companies operate in — and therefore matters for investors in the space.

stories.title: iOS 27 could let iPhone users swap out ChatGPT for Gemini or Claude
stories.why_it_matters: Reports suggest Apple's upcoming iOS 27 may allow iPhone users to replace ChatGPT (the current default AI assistant) with rivals like Google's Gemini or Anthropic's Claude. This would be a significant move — Apple currently has around 1.5 billion active devices globally, so whichever AI gets chosen as the default assistant gains enormous reach. For Google in particular (GOOG), having Gemini available as a first-class option on iPhones would be a major commercial win.

sport.summary: Big NRL Round 27 action over the weekend, with the Raiders hammering the Cowboys 50-30 and the Rabbitohs smashing the Roosters 50-20. A drama-filled Sharks vs Storm game saw a Melbourne winger stretchered off. In AFL, the finals are heating up with Patrick Dangerfield and Geelong making headlines.

stories.title: Raiders demolish Cowboys 50-30; Rabbitohs thrash Roosters 50-20
stories.why_it_matters: Two massive Round 27 results on Saturday: the Raiders ran riot over the Cowboys 50-30 in Townsville — a statement win for Canberra with finals implications. On Friday night, the Rabbitohs put up 50 points against the Roosters in a dominant 50-20 performance at Allianz Stadium — a huge result in the Sydney rivalry. The Broncos also got up over the Bulldogs 34-20 on Thursday night.

stories.title: Melbourne Storm winger stretchered off in sin-bin drama against Sharks
stories.why_it_matters: Saturday night's Sharks vs Storm game at Ocean Protect Stadium ended 24-20 to Melbourne, but was marred by controversy. A Storm winger was stretchered off and taken to hospital during the match — serious injury concerns for Melbourne. Two players were also sin-binned (sent to the sin bin for 10 minutes) after a flare-up on the field. Melbourne Storm hold on for the win but the injury cloud is a major concern heading into the finals.

stories.title: Dolphins edge Titans 24-20 in controversial Gold Coast clash
stories.why_it_matters: The Dolphins beat the Titans 24-20 in a fiery Gold Coast derby on Friday night that sparked controversy — an NRL great publicly erupted over what they called a 'shocking decision' by the referee at a crucial moment. The game was filled with controversy and tempers. For local Gold Coast fans, the Titans' loss at home will sting, while the Dolphins continue their climb up the table.

stories.title: Warriors edge Sea Eagles 31-30 in Saturday thriller
stories.why_it_matters: The New Zealand Warriors held off a fast-finishing Manly Sea Eagles 31-30 in a heart-stopper at Go Media Stadium in Auckland on Saturday afternoon. Just one point separated the sides at full time — a dramatic finish in what shapes as a finals preview with both teams in the hunt.

stories.title: Geelong's stunning comeback features Dangerfield heroics in AFL finals
stories.why_it_matters: The AFL finals are in full swing, and Geelong pulled off a stunning comeback that has the football world buzzing. Patrick Dangerfield was at the centre of an extraordinary act during the win — described as historic scenes by reporters — while Sydney's Charlie also made a major impact. The Swans player ratings from the game hint at a close, fiercely contested finals series emerging.
